doc.title: Arturo Sandoval interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 12, 2023

title: Playing piano to improve trumpet improvisation
summary: He explains the Dizzy and Miles piano story and why he spends more time at the piano, where he can see chords.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You just answered one of the questions I had written down, so thank you. Does the fact that you play piano impact your trumpet improvising?

Big time, and a great question. That was, after I listened to that, later on I got in my hands one of those jazz history books. And in one of the chapters of that book it was the story of Miles Davis came to Dizzy Gillespie asking him for help to get into the more deeper concept of improvisation and knowledge of the changes and all those things. And Dizzy said, “Okay I can help you. Let’s go to the piano.” And Miles said, “Piano? What?” Dizzy said, “Okay, that’s the only way I can explain it to you.” When I read that, hold on let me close the door because my wife is start talking. And when I read that I said uh oh, I think that’s a good lesson, not only for Miles, that’s good for everyone. And then that

really made that thing into my brain and I said you know what? I have to get familiar with the piano. And I never regret it. By the way, I spend a lot more time with the piano than with the trumpet. Because the piano for composition, for arranging, for creating, for understanding the chord sequencing and the basis, not only the basis but only all the variation and a tentative chord that you can find, and the piano has something else that is you can hear the thing but you can see. You understand what I mean? With the trumpet you cannot see anything. You have to imagine everything — or clarinet or a saxophone or whatever. But with the piano you can see the notes that belongs to the chord and what are the changes you can do with that and what are the scales that belongs to that specific chord. And then that gives you a better control, a better conscious of how to handle those chord changes.

That’s a terrific observation. Because I play saxophone and piano and I noticed that sometimes if I see, you know, talking about notes that are outside the scale, playing outside a little bit. And you’re right, there’s a visual dimension to it, you know?
